lesson.grammar_point: present perfect with just, already and yet

listenings.text: Before I travel to meet a local team, my analysts have already read everything that is public: the contract, the regulator's decisions, the news. So I do not need a long presentation. In the first meeting I ask three questions. What has already been approved? What has not happened yet? And what has changed in the last month? A team that answers those three questions in ten minutes gets a second meeting. We have just finished a process in Chile, and the team there did exactly that. They even sent the minutes before I got back to the hotel.

I have worked with foreign funds for about fifteen years, and I have learned one thing. When an investor pushes back, do not argue in the room. Last year we had a client who wanted to defend every point of the term sheet. After two meetings, nobody had moved. In the third meeting we changed the approach. We agreed on the facts first, we wrote them on the board, and we checked that everybody was on the same page. The deal has not closed yet, but the discussion is much faster now, and the fund has already asked for a new draft.

reading.rtitle: The First Meeting With the Fund
paras: When a foreign pension fund looks at a project in Brazil, the first meeting is rarely about money. The fund has usually already read the public documents, and its team has already talked to one or two local advisers. What it wants to know in the room is simpler: where is the project today, and what could stop it tomorrow? A good local team answers with facts, not with promises.

The best answers are short and precise. The regulator has already approved the plan. The environmental license has not been issued yet, but the hearing is next month. We have just received the first draft of the concession contract. In three sentences, the investor knows what is finished, what is still open and what has changed this week. A long presentation often says less.

Investors also push back, and a Brazilian team should expect it. The most common questions are about deadlines and about the regulator. A lawyer who has worked on both sides says the key is not to defend every point. It is to agree on the facts first, make sure everybody is on the same page, and then follow up in writing the same day, with the minutes and a clear list of next steps.
